questions.q: What makes every person's life genuinely one-of-a-kind, according to lesson 1?
a: An unrepeatable mix of genes and personal experiences
A hidden talent that no one else can ever develop
A fixed destiny decided at the moment of birth
A unique score on standardized intelligence tests
questions.why: Lesson 1 says no one has had your biology or your exact circumstances.

questions.q: Why do so many people end up following the same career path?
a: Fear of the unknown pushes them toward society's safe plan
Schools collect data and assign students to needed jobs
Most people genuinely share the same talents and interests
Employers only hire graduates from a single program
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the brain craves certainty, and society offers a familiar script.

questions.q: How does Robinson suggest we treat the unknown?
a: Look for the opportunities it might reveal instead of dreading it
Reduce it by planning every decade of your life in advance
Avoid it until you have enough experience to handle it
Accept that nothing good can come from uncertainty
questions.why: Lesson 2 points out that many good things can emerge from an open future.

questions.q: Which kind of intelligence does the school system mainly reward?
a: Logical reasoning of the kind measured by IQ
Creative expression through dance and music
Practical skills learned outside the classroom
Emotional awareness in group situations
questions.why: Lesson 3 says math and science sit at the top while the arts sit at the bottom.

questions.q: How does the book suggest uncovering a hidden talent?
a: Revisit what teachers once told you that you were bad at
Take the subjects you scored highest in and double down
Copy the career of the most successful person you know
Wait until your talents become obvious on their own
questions.why: Lesson 3 says school may have discouraged the very thing you would love.
